excerpt: I got banned from Lobsters for writing like an LLM I've been banned from Lobsters. If you're bored, you can read about my experience. If you don't know it, Lobsters is a news aggregator focused on technology and computing, although other topics of general interest also come up. The most interesting part is the comments on each thread or link, where the topics are discussed. As alternatives, there are Hacker News, Lemmy and, to some extent, Reddit. To give you some background, I've been a Lobsters user for a few years. I've contributed comments and links, and I'm also the author of the Emacs client. On top of that, the IRC channel I hang out in the most is #lobsters on Libera.Chat. Chapter 1: Your domain has been blocked A year ago, around Christmas 2025, I tried to share an article on Lobsters. My usual style, educational but fun. When I did, I ran into a warning telling me that my website's domain was blocked for self-promotion. My domain? This surprised me, since I hadn't shared content from my website on Lobsters before, and I had read the odd unhappy comment. But blocking the whole domain seemed a bit much. I didn't make a big deal of it! I sent an email to the moderators explaining the situation. I got no reply. Chapter 2: Contributing again Almost a year later, with a few articles on the Hacker News front page, I thought about Lobsters again. I decided to contribute again with a simple post: my experience building a modern BBS. Improvements over older systems like BBJ, and an explanation of some design decisions. It ended with an invitation to try it, and I shared it with the show tag. Nothing more. Same result: domain blocked for self-promotion. They hadn't lifted the block after a year, and they never answered my message. I didn't make a big deal of it. By chance, I found a way to post a blocked domain. It looked like a small bug. I was posting again after a year in exile. Chapter 3: The rise Little by little, the points went up and the comments came in…
